editorial.titleTr: 스탠포드 한국센터에 낭비된 한국 납세자 돈 1230만 달러
summaryTr: 한국이 스탠포드 센터 코리아 운영에 납세자 자금 1,230만 달러를 낭비했다.
인천자유경제구역 시설은 예상된 수익을 창출하지 못했다.
사설은 국제교육 투자 부실 관리에 대한 책임 추궁을 요구한다.
editorial.bodyTr:
인천자유경제구역(IFEZ)에는 세계적 수준의 외국 교육 및 연구 기관들의 국제 캠퍼스가 위치하고 있습니다. 국제 협력의 허브로서 기능하는 이곳은 한국과 세계를 연결하는 중요한 역할을 담당하고 있습니다. 그러나 최근 이러한 국제 교육 기관들이 직면한 여러 도전 과제들이 대두되고 있습니다.

이들 기관의 성공적인 운영과 발전을 위해서는 정부와 지방 자치단체의 지속적인 지원과 관심이 필수적입니다. 국제 경쟁력을 갖춘 교육 환경 조성, 외국인 유학생들을 위한 편의 시설 개선, 그리고 현지 인재와의 교류 활성화 등이 필요합니다.

IFEZ의 국제 교육 허브로서의 위상을 더욱 강화하기 위해서는 단순한 물리적 인프라 구축을 넘어 질적 수준의 개선이 요구됩니다. 외국 기관들이 한국에서 뿌리내리고 성장할 수 있도록 하는 포용적이고 지원적인 환경 조성이 시급합니다.

결국 IFEZ의 발전은 인천뿐 아니라 한국 전체의 국제적 위상 강화와 교육 경쟁력 향상으로 이어질 것입니다. 이를 위해 관계자 모두가 함께 노력해야 할 시점입니다.

editorials.titleTr: [Editorial] Broadening Its Base to Challenge the Administration, the Democratic Party Must First Embrace Oh Se-hoon, Han Dong-hun, and Lee Jun-seok
summaryTr: The People Power Party has embarked on rallying conservatives and expanding its base.
It is essential to embrace influential figures such as Oh Se-hoon, Han Dong-hoon, and Lee Jun-seok.
As the opposition party, it must strengthen its capacity to check the government in power.
editorials.bodyTr:
The ruling party faces a critical juncture as it attempts to consolidate conservative support while expanding its political base. Party Chairman Jang Dong-hyeok's strategy requires urgent recalibration to move beyond the divisive politics of subtraction that has characterized recent internal dynamics.

The party's current approach of exclusion has proven counterproductive. Rather than strengthening the conservative bloc, the practice of sidelining prominent figures has only fragmented the vote and weakened the party's capacity to function as an effective opposition force. This narrowing of ranks contradicts the imperatives of political survival in an increasingly competitive electoral landscape.

The time has come for the party to embrace inclusion. Figures such as Oh Se-hoon, Han Dong-hun, and Lee Jun-seok represent significant political assets whose talents and constituencies cannot be dismissed without consequence. Their reintegration into the party structure would not signal weakness or compromise of principle, but rather demonstrate the political maturity necessary to build a formidable opposition capable of holding government accountable.

The party's role as a check on executive power depends fundamentally on its ability to mobilize resources and present a unified alternative vision. This requires moving beyond personality conflicts and factional disputes to focus on the substantive work of opposition governance. Only through such expansion can the conservative movement hope to regain public confidence and rebuild the institutional strength necessary for future political competition.

editorials.titleTr: Opinion: Are Documents Found After Martial Law Lifting Evidence of Insurrection? Isn't This Fabricated Prosecution?
summaryTr: The second independent counsel's office has indicted former Prosecutor General Shim Woo-jung on charges related to martial law.
Key evidence documents were revealed to have actually been created after the martial law was lifted.
Controversy over the validity of the investigation and the possibility of prosecutorial manipulation is spreading.
editorials.bodyTr: The second comprehensive special investigation into Gwon Chang-young has indicted former Prosecutor General Shim Woo-jung on suspicion of being dispatched as a prosecutor to the Martial Law Joint Investigation Headquarters during the emergency martial law period. However, key documentary evidence has been confirmed to actually be a list intended for the Prosecution's Special Investigation Division created after martial law was lifted, raising controversy over the validity of the investigation and the possibility of evidence manipulation.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Jang Dong-hyuk Trapped by Hardcore Fandom, Lee Jun-seok Steps Back...Conservatives Face Rough Road to Rebuilding
summaryTr: People Power Party leader Jang Dong-hyeok has failed to present a vision for conservative reconstruction, relying solely on hardcore supporters.
Reform New Party leader Lee Jun-seok resigned taking responsibility for defeat in local elections, revealing setbacks in the third-way experiment.
The collapse of opposition trust has led to the ruling party's unchecked dominance, making innovative conservative reconstruction an essential task for democratic stability.
editorial.bodyTr: On the day PPP Chairman Jang Dong-hyuk held a press conference marking his first anniversary in office, Reform Party Chairman Lee Jun-seok announced his resignation. It was a scene of stark contrast between the two pillars of the conservative opposition. Chairman Jang expressed his ambition to make a fresh start for victory in the 2028 general election. He declared that he would strengthen the party's competitive power through expanding party member sovereignty and recruiting talented figures capable of putting up a real fight, thereby laying the groundwork for electoral victory. However, suspicions persist within the party about whether this amounts to placing loyalists in key positions. To dispel such doubts, Chairman Jang must demonstrate the ability to expand the opposition's political spectrum beyond narrow factional unity appealing to hardcore supporters. Chairman Jang also stated he would become "the big brother of conservatism," but he offered no concrete reform measures on what he would do or how to rebuild collapsed conservative leadership. He promised to establish a "Conservative Identity Establishment Committee," but this falls short of meeting public expectations for fundamental conservative renewal. Lee's resignation over responsibility for the defeat in the June 3 local elections and the party's failure to strengthen and reform itself reflects how the conservative opposition is losing its way without presenting a vision and leadership as an alternative force. Although Lee once commanded the spotlight with high name recognition and political instincts appealing to younger generations, he failed to expand this into a sustainable organizational and support base. The third-way experiment in reform-minded conservatism has thus encountered a setback. The impact of this conservative political crisis extends beyond the defeat of a particular party or the diminished standing of individual politicians. If the opposition party, which should check the ruling party's quasi-monopoly of the legislature, loses credibility, the damage reverberates to the people and the entire democratic system. Without a healthy alternative force, the ruling party's high-handedness and arrogance intensify, and policy mistakes cannot be corrected. This is why urgent reconstruction of a healthy conservative opposition is imperative. The message from voters in the local elections was clear: stop wasteful internal strife, undertake renewal on a fundamental level, and break free from isolation dependent on hardcore supporters. Only then can the party win the hearts of swing voters and the moderate middle ground. Moving beyond ideological frameworks to represent young people and social minorities while broadening its base is the starting point for reconstruction. Democracy flies straight only on two wings—conservatism and progressivism. That task rests with the conservative political establishment.

editorial.title: Historical populism
editorial.body: North Jeolla’s plan to pay descendants of Donghak participants sets troubling precedent The government of North Jeolla Province in southwestern Korea will reportedly pay an annual allowance of 1.2 million won ($868) to each of 723 family members of participants in the Donghak Peasant Revolution, which took place 132 years ago. The government is using taxpayers’ money to provide cash payments to the great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren of participants in the revolution, as descendants of victims of the historic event of 1894-1895. The Donghak Peasant Revolution was a popular uprising against feudalism and foreign powers, sparked by local officials’ exploitative taxation and ruthless rule. The uprising prompted military intervention by China and Japan and ultimately led to the First Sino-Japanese War. The very idea of digging up history as far back as the late Joseon period to create a sort of veterans’ allowance is simply absurd. Even more astonishing is the dire financial situation facing the provincial government. In 2024, North Jeolla’s fiscal self-reliance ratio stood at 23.51 percent, the lowest among the country’s 16 metropolitan cities and provinces. Its own revenue is barely enough to cover the salaries of its civil servants, and the province is now deeply in debt after issuing local government bonds to make up for a budget shortfall. Moreover, North Jeolla Province has forced the cities and counties under its jurisdiction to shoulder 70 percent of the cost of these allowances. The financial situation is even worse at the city and county level: Most, with the exception of Jeonju, had fiscal self-reliance ratios below 20 percent, while Jinan County ranked last among the country’s local governments at just 6.69 percent. The decision to pay the allowance sets a dangerous precedent that undermines the nation’s veterans’ benefits system. Even the Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs has opposed granting official honors to participants in the Donghak revolution, citing a lack of academic consensus and the risk of confusion with independence activists officially honored by the government. The Democratic Party of Korea has been relentless in its push to grant special recognition and benefits to participants in the Donghak Peasant Revolution, which began in North Jeolla Province, one of its political strongholds. The relevant special law was enacted in 2004, and the Roh Moo-hyun administration began accepting applications to register participants and bereaved family members. When applications remained low, it expanded the scope of eligible bereaved family members in 2007 to include even great-great-grandchildren. If this is how historical events are to be recognized, there is reason to restore the honor of the farmers who rose up against corrupt officials in Jinju, South Gyeongsang Province, more than 30 years before the Donghak Peasant Revolution. By the same logic, allowances would have to be paid to the bereaved families of peasants who took up arms against corrupt officials around the turn of the 20th century — and perhaps even to the descendants of those who fought Japanese invaders during the 1592 invasion of Joseon. When it comes to Korea’s independence movement, it is only reasonable to limit official government compensation to those who contributed to the movement after Korea came under Japanese colonial rule. The government could go further back in time, but it would become increasingly difficult to identify those involved, locate their descendants who are alive, and reach agreement on how the events should be assessed. The Donghak Peasant Revolution is already taught in school textbooks. Memorial towers and monuments have also been erected at major historic sites. Their honor has already been restored. Yet this financially strapped North Jeolla plans to pay allowances to the descendants of those who participated in a popular uprising more than 130 years ago. This is an exploitation of history for populist ends, giving the Donghak Peasant Revolution preferential treatment over other historical events. 한국 남서부 지역의 전라북도 정부가 132년 전 일어난 동학농민혁명 참여자 723명의 가족들에게 연간 120만 원의 수당을 지급할 계획이라고 보도되었다. 정부는 1894~1895년의 역사적 사건 피해자 후손들로서 혁명 참여자들의 5대, 6대 손자·손녀들에게 현금을 지급하기 위해 납세자의 세금을 사용하고 있다. 동학농민혁명은 봉건제도와 외세에 저항한 대중적 봉기로, 지역 관료들의 착취적 과세와 독재적 통치에서 촉발되었다. 이 봉기는 중국과 일본의 군사적 개입을 초래했고 궁극적으로 제1차 중일전쟁으로 이어졌다.

조선 말기까지 거슬러 올라가는 역사를 파헤쳐 일종의 참전용사 수당을 만들자는 발상 자체가 황당하다. 더욱 놀라운 것은 도청의 극심한 재정난이다. 2024년 전라북도의 재정자립도는 23.51%로 전국 16개 광역시·도 중 가장 낮다. 자체 세입만으로는 공무원 급여를 간신히 충당할 수 있을 정도이며, 예산 부족을 메우기 위해 지방채를 발행한 후 도는 심각한 빚에 빠져 있다. 더욱이 전라북도는 이 수당 비용의 70%를 산하 시군에 떠넘겼다. 시군 단위의 재정 상황은 더욱 열악하다. 전주를 제외한 대부분이 재정자립도 20% 미만이며, 지난군은 6.69%로 전국 지방자치단체 중 가장 낮다.

이 수당 지급 결정은 국가의 참전용사 복지 체계를 훼손하는 위험한 선례를 남긴다. 국가보훈처마저 동학농민혁명 참여자에 대한 공식 추모를 반대하고 있으며, 학계의 합의 부족과 정부가 공식으로 인정한 독립운동가와의 혼동 위험을 이유로 들고 있다. 민주당은 자신의 정치적 강세 지역 중 하나인 전라북도에서 시작된 동학농민혁명 참여자들에 대한 특별 인정과 혜택을 부여하기 위해 끊임없이 추진해 왔다. 관련 특별법은 2004년 제정되었고, 노무현 정부는 참여자와 유족 등록 신청을 받기 시작했다. 신청이 저조하자 2007년 적격 유족의 범위를 확대하여 5대 손자·손녀까지 포함시켰다.

역사 사건을 이런 식으로 인정한다면, 동학농민혁명이 일어나기 30년 이상 전에 경상남도 진주에서 부패 관료에 저항하여 일어난 농민들의 명예를 회복할 이유가 있다. 같은 논리로라면 20세기 초 부패 관료에 저항하여 무기를 들었던 농민들의 유족, 나아가 1592년 도요토미 히데요시의 임진왜란 때 일본 침략군에 저항한 자들의 후손에게도 수당을 지급해야 할 것이다. 한국의 독립운동에 관해서라면, 정부 보상을 한반도가 일본 식민지배를 받은 이후 독립운동에 기여한 자들로 한정하는 것이 타당하다. 정부가 더 오래 전으로 거슬러 올라갈 수도 있지만, 관여자를 파악하고, 생존한 후손을 찾아내고, 역사 사건을 어떻게 평가할 것인지 합의에 이르기는 점점 더 어려워질 것이다.

동학농민혁명은 이미 학교 교과서에 실려 있고, 주요 역사 유적지에는 추모탑과 기념비도 세워져 있다. 그들의 명예는 이미 회복되었다. 그런데 재정이 어려운 전라북도가 130년 이상 전의 민중 봉기 참여자들의 후손에게 수당을 지급하려고 한다. 이는 역사를 대중영합적 목적으로 악용하는 것이며, 동학농민혁명에 다른 역사 사건보다 우대를 해주는 것이다.

editorials.title: Historical populism
editorials.body: North Jeolla’s plan to pay descendants of Donghak participants sets troubling precedent The government of North Jeolla Province in southwestern Korea will reportedly pay an annual allowance of 1.2 million won ($868) to each of 723 family members of participants in the Donghak Peasant Revolution, which took place 132 years ago. The government is using taxpayers’ money to provide cash payments to the great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren of participants in the revolution, as descendants of victims of the historic event of 1894-1895. The Donghak Peasant Revolution was a popular uprising against feudalism and foreign powers, sparked by local officials’ exploitative taxation and ruthless rule. The uprising prompted military intervention by China and Japan and ultimately led to the First Sino-Japanese War. The very idea of digging up history as far back as the late Joseon period to create a sort of veterans’ allowance is simply absurd. Even more astonishing is the dire financial situation facing the provincial government. In 2024, North Jeolla’s fiscal self-reliance ratio stood at 23.51 percent, the lowest among the country’s 16 metropolitan cities and provinces. Its own revenue is barely enough to cover the salaries of its civil servants, and the province is now deeply in debt after issuing local government bonds to make up for a budget shortfall. Moreover, North Jeolla Province has forced the cities and counties under its jurisdiction to shoulder 70 percent of the cost of these allowances. The financial situation is even worse at the city and county level: Most, with the exception of Jeonju, had fiscal self-reliance ratios below 20 percent, while Jinan County ranked last among the country’s local governments at just 6.69 percent. The decision to pay the allowance sets a dangerous precedent that undermines the nation’s veterans’ benefits system. Even the Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs has opposed granting official honors to participants in the Donghak revolution, citing a lack of academic consensus and the risk of confusion with independence activists officially honored by the government. The Democratic Party of Korea has been relentless in its push to grant special recognition and benefits to participants in the Donghak Peasant Revolution, which began in North Jeolla Province, one of its political strongholds. The relevant special law was enacted in 2004, and the Roh Moo-hyun administration began accepting applications to register participants and bereaved family members. When applications remained low, it expanded the scope of eligible bereaved family members in 2007 to include even great-great-grandchildren. If this is how historical events are to be recognized, there is reason to restore the honor of the farmers who rose up against corrupt officials in Jinju, South Gyeongsang Province, more than 30 years before the Donghak Peasant Revolution. By the same logic, allowances would have to be paid to the bereaved families of peasants who took up arms against corrupt officials around the turn of the 20th century — and perhaps even to the descendants of those who fought Japanese invaders during the 1592 invasion of Joseon. When it comes to Korea’s independence movement, it is only reasonable to limit official government compensation to those who contributed to the movement after Korea came under Japanese colonial rule. The government could go further back in time, but it would become increasingly difficult to identify those involved, locate their descendants who are alive, and reach agreement on how the events should be assessed. The Donghak Peasant Revolution is already taught in school textbooks. Memorial towers and monuments have also been erected at major historic sites. Their honor has already been restored. Yet this financially strapped North Jeolla plans to pay allowances to the descendants of those who participated in a popular uprising more than 130 years ago. This is an exploitation of history for populist ends, giving the Donghak Peasant Revolution preferential treatment over other historical events.
